summary: Gives a history and description of the Internet Activities Board and its subsidiary organizations. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1160.

plainLanguage.summary: This tells the story of the group that guided the Internet and the smaller teams working under it.

questions: what is the internet activities board
subtitle: The coordinating body for internet design, engineering, and management in 1989.

tldr.problem: As the internet grew in the late 1980s, there was a need for a coordinating body to guide its technical development and governance across multiple research communities and government agencies.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Activities Board (IAB) was established as the coordinating committee for Internet design, engineering, and management, with two subsidiary task forces: the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) for near-term engineering and the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF) for longer-term research.
tldr.outcome: The IAB became the central authority for setting Internet standards, managing the RFC publication process, and coordinating development of the TCP/IP protocol suite, establishing a governance structure that evolved into the modern IETF and IRTF.

today: RFC 1120 is an Informational RFC documenting the IAB, IETF, and IRTF as they existed in September 1989, and was obsoleted by RFC 1160. The governance structures described in this RFC evolved significantly over subsequent decades. Today the IETF and IRTF continue as the principal bodies for Internet engineering and research, though their structure and leadership have changed substantially.

sections.title: The Birth of Internet Governance
sections.content:
By the late 1970s, the ARPANET research project had grown beyond a handful of researchers tinkering with packet-switching protocols. In 1979, an informal committee called the Internet Configuration Control Board (ICCB) was formed under Dr. Vinton Cerf, with Dr. David C. Clark of MIT as chairman, to guide the technical evolution of the protocol suite.

In January 1983, the Defense Communications Agency declared the TCP/IP protocol suite standard for the ARPANET, and all connected systems were converted from the earlier Network Control Program (NCP) to TCP/IP. Later that year, the ICCB was reorganized around technical task forces and renamed the Internet Activities Board (IAB). This new structure reflected the internet's growth and the need for coordinated engineering across multiple research communities, universities, and government agencies including DARPA, the National Science Foundation (NSF), the Department of Energy (DOE), and NASA.
sections.plainLanguage: The internet started as a small experiment but grew so fast that scientists realized they needed a main committee to make decisions about how it should work. The ICCB was born in 1979, renamed to the IAB in 1983, and it became the top decision-making body.

sections.title: The IAB and Its Mission
sections.content:
The Internet Activities Board is an independent committee of researchers and professionals with a technical interest in the health and evolution of the Internet system. All IAB members are required to have at least one other major role in the Internet community beyond IAB membership, ensuring they remain grounded in active work.

The IAB performs six core functions: setting Internet standards, managing the RFC publication process (which had been running since 1969), reviewing the operation of subsidiary task forces, performing strategic planning for the Internet, acting as a technical policy liaison for the Internet community, and resolving technical issues that cannot be handled within the task forces.

The RFC series, managed by the IAB through editor Jonathan Postel, is the primary vehicle for publishing IAB decisions and technical work. The IAB meets quarterly to review the internet's condition, approve proposed protocol changes, set development priorities, discuss policy matters with government sponsors, and manage committee membership.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB is the main decision-making team that decides what rules the internet should follow. It runs the famous RFC publication system (the way engineers share ideas), and members must be working on real internet problems in addition to being on the committee.

sections.title: The IETF and IRTF: Doing the Work
sections.content:
The IAB delegates its work through two principal subsidiary task forces:

The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), chaired by Phillip Gross and managed by the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG), handles the short and mid-term engineering challenges. The IETF is organized around eight technical areas, each with a technical area director, and works through more than 20 Working Groups focused on specific problems. The IETF is where protocol standards are proposed, debated, and refined before IAB approval.

The Internet Research Task Force (IRTF), chaired by David Clark, is concerned with longer-term research rather than near-term products. While there is overlap in membership between the two (for cross-fertilization and technology transfer), the IRTF generally focuses on understanding rather than standards. It is organized into Research Groups covering broad areas such as end-to-end services, autonomous networks, privacy and security, and user interfaces.

The IAB also coordinates with international bodies through the Federal Research Internet Coordinating Committee (FRICC) in the United States and the Coordinating Committee for Intercontinental Research Networks (CCIRN), which includes North American and European research networking bodies.
sections.plainLanguage: Under the IAB are two working teams. The IETF builds things that work now—protocols and standards. The IRTF thinks about the future and tries out new ideas. Both teams have researchers from universities and government agencies all working together.

sections.title: The IAB's Near-Term Agenda
sections.content:
In 1989, the IAB identified seven principal focus areas for 1989 and 1990: operational stability of the internet, user services (particularly electronic directory and email), OSI protocol coexistence, testbed facilities, security, handling growth to millions of users, and supporting gigabit-speed networks.

The document recommended specific actions including improved operational tools and fault isolation, standardization of interior gateway routing protocols by vendors, adoption of Host Requirements RFCs, deployment of White Pages directory services, privacy-enhanced email, development of user services like X.500, and multi-protocol support and interoperability testing. These priorities set the agenda for internet development in the years that followed.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB in 1989 was worried about keeping the internet reliable and fast, making it easy for people to use email, connecting to other kinds of networks, and supporting gigantic computers and huge numbers of users. Most of these problems got solved in the following years.
